title_en: Lacoste (France) Co., Ltd. v. Crocodile International Private Limited (Singapore) and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Garments Co., Ltd., Beijing Branch — dispute over trademark infringement
ruling_gist_en: Article 9, Paragraph 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks stipulates: 'The similarity of trademarks as referred to in Item (1) of Article 52 of the Trademark Law means that, when comparing the allegedly infringing trademark with the plaintiff's registered trademark, the shapes, pronunciations, or meanings of the characters, or the composition and colors of the figures, or the overall structure after combination of their elements, or the three-dimensional shapes or color combinations are similar, such that it is likely to cause the relevant public to be mistaken about the source of the goods or to believe that the source has a specific connection with the goods of the plaintiff's registered trademark.' Therefore, trademark similarity in the sense of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark refers to confusing similarity, that is, similarity sufficient to cause market confusion. In determining trademark similarity based on the specific circumstances of the trademark in dispute, in addition to the usual consideration of the degree of similarity of its constituent elements, it is also necessary to comprehensively consider other relevant factors, such as the subjective intent of the alleged infringer, the history and current status of coexistence and use by both parties, the actual market situation, and other factors. On this basis, a fair and reasonable judgment shall be made to determine whether the trademark in dispute constitutes confusing similarity. If the trademark in dispute is similar only in its constituent elements, but after comprehensive consideration of other relevant factors it cannot be determined to be sufficient to cause market confusion, it shall not be deemed to infringe the exclusive right to use a registered trademark.

full_text_en:
Lacoste SA (France) v. Crocodile International Pte Ltd (Singapore) and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Garments Co., Ltd. Beijing Branch — dispute over infringement of trademark exclusive right

【Ruling Summary】

Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks provides: "The similarity of trademarks under Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law refers to similarity between the allegedly infringing trademark and the plaintiff's registered trademark in terms of the shape, pronunciation, or meaning of the words, or the composition and color of the graphics, or the overall structure after combination of their elements, or the similarity of their three-dimensional shapes or color combinations, which is likely to cause the relevant public to be confused about the source of the goods or to believe that the source is specifically related to the source of the goods under the plaintiff's registered trademark." Therefore, similarity of trademarks in the context of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark refers to confusing similarity, that is, similarity sufficient to cause market confusion. When determining trademark similarity based on the specific circumstances of the disputed trademarks, in addition to the usual consideration of the degree of similarity of their constituent elements, it is also necessary to comprehensively consider other relevant factors, such as the subjective intent of the alleged infringer, the history and current situation of coexistence and use of both parties, and the actual market conditions. On this basis, a fair and reasonable judgment shall be made to determine whether the disputed trademarks constitute confusing similarity. If the disputed trademarks are similar only in their constituent elements, but after comprehensively considering other relevant factors, it cannot be determined that they are sufficient to cause market confusion, then they shall not be found to infringe the exclusive right to use a registered trademark.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court
(2009) Min San Zhong Zi No. 3

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Lacoste SA (LACOSTE), France, domiciled at 8, Rue de Castiglione, 75001 Paris, France.
Legal Representative: Michel Lacoste, Chairman of the Board of Directors.
Agent ad litem: Huang Yibiao, attorney at Beijing Wanhuida Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Gao Chao, attorney at Beijing Hanting United Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Crocodile International Pte Ltd, Singapore, domiciled at Crocodile House, 3 Ubi Avenue 3, Singapore.
Legal Representative: Ang Boon Tiang, Chairman of the Board of Directors.
Agent ad litem: Tao Xinliang, attorney at Beijing Dentons Law Offices, LLP Shanghai Branch.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Garments Co., Ltd. Beijing Branch, domiciled at Ground Floor, Building B, No. 18 Gongti East Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.
Responsible Person: Yan Zhongliang, General Manager.
Agent ad litem: Tao Xinliang, attorney at Beijing Dentons Law Offices, LLP Shanghai Branch.

The appellant, Lacoste SA (France) (hereinafter "Lacoste"), having appealed against the civil judgment (2000) Gao Min Chu Zi No. 29 of the Beijing High People's Court of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "the court of first instance") in the dispute over infringement of the exclusive right to use a trademark with the respondents, Crocodile International Pte Ltd (Singapore) (hereinafter "Crocodile International") and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Garments Co., Ltd. Beijing Branch (hereinafter "Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Company"), has filed an appeal with this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, composed of Xia Junli, judge of the Third Civil Adjudication Tribunal, as presiding judge, judges Yin Shaoping and Wang Yanfang, acting judge, with court clerk Bao Shuo keeping the record. The case was heard in an open session. Attorneys Huang Yibiao and Gao Chao, agents ad litem for the appellant Lacoste, and attorney Tao Xinliang, the common agent ad litem for the respondents Crocodile International and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Company, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case has now been concluded.

The court of first instance found the following facts upon trial: Lacoste was founded in 1933 and registered the "crocodile graphic" trademark in France in the same year. Thereafter, its products were mainly sold in Europe. In the 1960s, Lacoste began to promote its products to Asia. In the late 1970s, its products entered Hong Kong. In 1980, Lacoste registered the "crocodile graphic" trademark in Mainland China, and its products officially entered China in 1984, but in limited quantities. In 1994, Lacoste officially opened counters or specialty stores. On May 11, 2000, Lacoste filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, alleging that since 1980, it had successively registered a series of "crocodile graphic" trademarks in China, and according to Chinese law, it had the exclusive right to use the registered "crocodile graphic" trademarks. In 1995, Lacoste discovered that Crocodile International had established multiple stores in China, with realistic-style crocodile graphics on their signs, selling clothing products bearing the "crocodile graphic" trademark. Lacoste issued warnings to Crocodile International in 1995 and 1998. Furthermore, Crocodile International and its agent in Beijing, Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Company, were still selling clothing and other related products bearing the "crocodile graphic" trademark in the Beijing area. The "crocodile graphic" trademarks used by the two defendants were similar to Lacoste's registered "crocodile graphic" trademarks, infringing on Lacoste's exclusive right to use its registered trademarks in Class 25 for clothing and other related classes, and violating the relevant provisions of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, Lacoste requested: (1) an order for the two defendants to cease the infringement, i.e., to stop using trademark identifiers similar to Lacoste's registered trademarks on identical or similar goods; (2) an order for the two defendants to compensate it for economic losses in the amount of RMB 3,000,000; (3) an order for the two defendants to eliminate the adverse effects; (4) an order for the two defendants to bear all litigation costs of this case.

The predecessor of Crocodile International was Lee Seng Ming Company, founded by Chen Xianjin in Singapore in 1943. The company applied for and was granted registration of the "crocodile + crocodile graphic" trademark in Singapore in 1951. Lee Seng Ming's products entered Hong Kong in 1953 and were mainly sold in Southeast Asia. In 1983, Lee Seng Ming changed its name to Crocodile International. In 1993, Crocodile International applied for registration of the "CARTELO and device" trademark in Mainland China, and its products entered the Chinese market in 1994. In 1969, Lee Seng Ming filed a civil lawsuit in the Osaka District Court in Japan, accusing Lacoste of trademark infringement. In 1973, the parties reached a settlement in the Osaka High Court, under which Lee Seng Ming agreed to allow Lacoste to register the "crocodile graphic" trademark in Japan. On June 17, 1983, the parties also entered into an agreement with the intent to: (1) terminate and finally settle all pending legal proceedings, legal actions, differences, disputes, and claims between them; (2) develop their own businesses; (3) jointly oppose third-party infringers; (4) cooperate in the countries listed in Article 1 of the agreement; (5) Lacoste agreed to pay compensation to Lee Seng Ming for past expenses for protection and defense of the "crocodile" trademark; (6) the parties agreed that their respective logos could coexist in the relevant markets without causing confusion; (7) the parties also intended to cooperate in other parts of the world if possible. In addition, the geographical scope agreed by the parties included Taiwan, China; Singapore; Indonesia; Malaysia; and Brunei.

It was further found that on October 30, 1980, Lacoste registered Trademark No. 141103, a "crocodile" graphic, in China, for use on goods in Class 25, clothing; on October 7, 1996, it registered Trademark No. 879258, a "crocodile" graphic, in China, for use on goods in Class 25, belts; on February 7, 1997, it registered Trademark No. 940231, "crocodile graphic + LACOSTE", in China, for use on goods in Class 18, leather and imitation leather, and goods made thereof, including leather bags, wallets, etc.; on September 28, 1999, it registered Trademark No. 1318589, a "crocodile" graphic, in China, for use on goods in Class 25, ties, shoes, etc. Crocodile International applied for Trademark No. 1331001, "CARTELO and device", with the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter “the Trademark Office”) on December 24, 1993, for use on goods in Class 25, clothing, suits, jackets, overcoats, leather garments, long leather coats, fur coats, underwear, briefs, undershirts, skirts, trousers, sports shirts, knitwear (clothing); and applied for Trademark No. 1343051, "CARTELO and device", on June 29, 1994, for use on goods in Class 18, leather, travel bags, wallets, bags for packaging (bags, pouches), umbrellas. The above two trademarks were ordered to be approved for registration by administrative judgments (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi Nos. 178 and 277 of the Beijing High People's Court on December 14, 2007, and these judgments have now become effective. Administrative judgment (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 178 found that, comparing Crocodile International's applied-for Trademark No. 1331001, "CARTELO and device", with Lacoste's lawfully held Trademark No. 141103, "crocodile graphic", the graphic parts of the two were similar, but the main parts and the overall structure after combining the elements were not identical or similar. When observed in isolation with the general attention of the relevant public, and considering the distinctiveness and reputation of Trademark No. 141103, there might be some association between the two, but there would be no confusion or mistaken belief. Administrative judgment (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 277 found that, comparing Crocodile International's applied-for Trademark No. 1343051, "CARTELO and device", with Lacoste's lawfully held Trademark No. 213407, "crocodile graphic + LACOSTE", the graphic parts of the two were similar, but the main parts and the overall structure after combining the elements were not identical or similar. When observed in isolation with the general attention of the relevant public and considering the distinctiveness and reputation of Trademark No. 213407, there might be some association between the two, but there would be no confusion or mistaken belief.

It was further found that on April 25, 2000, Lacoste purchased one "CARTELO crocodile T-shirt" produced by Crocodile International and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Company in Beijing, at a unit price of RMB 886 (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 1"). After the lawsuit was initiated, on July 29, 2002, Lacoste purchased in Beijing "CARTELO white shirt" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 2"), "CARTELO black leather bag" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 3"), "CARTELO jacket" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 4"), "CARTELO T-shirt" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 5"), "CARTELO trousers" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 6"), "CARTELO gift box" containing a tie, wallet, and belt (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 7"), and "CARTELO women's shoes" (hereinafter "Accused Infringing Product 8"). The accused infringing products 1-8 all bore the "CARTELO and device" trademark on their outer packaging and product hang tags. The accused infringing products 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 bore the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the collar or back waist; accused infringing product 7 (the tie inside the gift box) bore the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the back of the tie; accused infringing product 8 (women's shoes) bore the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the inner sole of the shoe. Accused infringing product 3 (the front of the leather bag) and accused infringing product 7 (the front of the wallet and the front of the belt buckle inside the gift box) bore the wording "CARTELO". Furthermore, accused infringing products 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 each bore the "crocodile graphic" trademark alone on the front chest or back waist; accused infringing product 3 and the wallet in the gift box (accused infringing product 7) each bore the "crocodile graphic" trademark alone on the front of the product; accused infringing product 7 (the tie inside the gift box) and accused infringing product 8 (the front of the product or the upper and sole of the shoe) each bore the "crocodile graphic" trademark alone; accused infringing product 7 (the belt inside the gift box) bore the "crocodile graphic" trademark alone on the front and back of the product.

In addition, by civil judgments that respectively took effect on October 22, 2005, December 20, 2005, and April 20, 2006, issued by the Changchun Intermediate People's Court of Jilin Province, People's Republic of China, (2005) Chang Min San Chu Zi No. 94; the Hubei High People's Court, People's Republic of China, (2005) E Min San Zhong Zi No. 9; and the Beijing High People's Court, (2006) Gao Min Zhong Zi No. 169, it was found that the sale of related goods solely bearing the "crocodile graphic" by Changchun Xinbaixin Commercial Trade Co., Ltd., Wuhan Martial Arts Group Co., Ltd. World Trade Plaza Shopping Center, and Beijing Xidan Scitech Mall Co., Ltd. infringed upon Lacoste's exclusive right to use its registered trademarks No. 141103, No. 879258, and No. 1318589.

In this case, Lacoste claimed that accused infringing products 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 infringed upon its registered trademark No. 141103 (crocodile graphic); accused infringing product 3 and the wallet in the gift box (accused infringing product 7) infringed upon its registered trademark No. 940231 (crocodile graphic + LACOSTE); the tie in the gift box (accused infringing product 7) and accused infringing product 8 infringed upon its registered trademark No. 1318589 (crocodile graphic); and the belt in the gift box (accused infringing product 7) infringed upon its registered trademark No. 879258 (crocodile graphic).

The court of first instance found upon trial that the legally effective administrative judgments (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi Nos. 178 and 277 of the Beijing High People's Court had confirmed the approval for registration of Crocodile International's applied-for trademarks No. 1331001 and No. 1343051, "CARTELO and device", filed on December 24, 1993, and June 29, 1994, and had found that the "CARTELO and device" trademarks and the "crocodile graphic" and "crocodile graphic + LACOSTE" trademarks would not cause confusion or mistaken belief. Therefore, the use of the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the outer packaging and product hang tags of the accused infringing products 1-8 in this case would not cause consumer confusion or mistaken belief with Lacoste's asserted registered trademarks No. 141103, No. 940231, No. 1318589, and No. 879258. That is, the use of the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the outer packaging and product hang tags of accused infringing products 1-8 produced by Crocodile International and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile Company did not infringe Lacoste's exclusive right to use its registered trademark. Similarly, the use of the wording "CARTELO" on the front of accused infringing product 3 (leather bag), the front of the wallet in the gift box (accused infringing product 7), and the front of the belt buckle would not cause consumer confusion or mistaken belief with the four registered trademarks asserted by Lacoste and did not infringe Lacoste's exclusive right to use its registered trademark.

Lacoste claimed that the accused infringing products 1-8 each bore the "crocodile graphic" alone on different parts, and compared with the crocodile graphics in the four registered trademarks asserted by the plaintiff, the only difference was that the direction of the crocodile's body was reversed, but the crocodile's posture was the same, mirror images, which was sufficient to cause confusion and mistaken belief among potential consumers during use after the sale of the accused infringing products. Regarding this, the court of first instance held that the trademark coexistence agreement reached between Lee Seng Ming and Lacoste on June 17, 1983, aimed to distinguish their respective products, was the genuine expression of the parties' intent, did not violate Chinese law, and did not harm the interests of others or the public interest. Therefore, it should be confirmed as effective. The agreement provided that the series of trademarks listed in Annexes 1 and 2 would "not cause confusion" in the regions of Taiwan, China; Singapore; Indonesia; Malaysia; and Brunei. In this case, Crocodile International's conduct was different from counterfeiting acts that deliberately imitate luxury brands. Crocodile International had no subjective intent to use Lacoste's brand reputation to cause consumer confusion or mistaken belief. After large-scale and long-term use in the Mainland Chinese market, Crocodile International's series of trademark identifiers had objectively established specific commercial reputation. Moreover, the accused infringing products 1-8 did not only bear the "crocodile graphic" but also bore "CARTELO" and "CARTELO and device". Taken as a whole, these gave the accused infringing products 1-8 an overall identity capable of effectively distinguishing them from other goods bearing crocodile images. In light of this, based on the principle of overall comparison and comprehensive assessment, the series of trademark identifiers of Lacoste and Crocodile International, as a whole, had formed significant distinguishing characteristics. Neither in the actual purchase of the goods nor in use after sale would they cause confusion or mistaken belief among consumers. The act of Crocodile International using the "crocodile graphic" alone on the accused infringing products 1-8 also did not infringe Lacoste's exclusive right to use its registered trademark. The civil judgments (2005) Chang Min San Chu Zi No. 94 of the Changchun Intermediate People's Court of Jilin Province, People's Republic of China; (2005) E Min San Zhong Zi No. 9 of the Hubei High People's Court, People's Republic of China; and (2006) Gao Min Zhong Zi No. 169 of the Beijing High People's Court involved different litigating parties, and the cases also differed in specific facts. Additionally, Crocodile International's trademarks No. 1331001 and No. 1343051, "CARTELO and device", which appeared on the outer packaging, product hang tags, and the products themselves, were approved for registration by the Beijing High People's Court on December 14, 2007, after those judgments became effective. Therefore, the above three judgments did not affect the trial of this case.

The court of first instance, in accordance with Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 10 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks, rendered a judgment on December 12, 2008, dismissing all of Lacoste's claims. Case acceptance fee was RMB 25,010, to be borne by Lacoste.

Lacoste, dissatisfied with the foregoing judgment, appealed to this Court, arguing: The "single crocodile figure" in the allegedly infringing trademark is identical to the appellant's crocodile trademark. The appellee's unauthorized use of a combined trademark containing a crocodile figure is similar to the appellant's registered trademark and constitutes trademark infringement. Both appellees' use of identical and similar trademarks on the same goods to the appellant's registered trademark is a typical act of trademark infringement. The first-instance judgment's finding of non-infringement is clearly erroneous. Specific reasons are as follows: 1. The allegedly infringing mark merely adds the foreign language "CARTELO" above the crocodile figure. In actual use, the relevant public would obviously more easily remember the familiar "crocodile" part and use it to memorize and refer to the mark. Since CARTELO is a foreign word with no meaning, for Chinese members of the public who are not familiar with foreign languages, when seeing the combined symbol of the CARTELO text and the crocodile figure, they would naturally take the crocodile figure as the memory part, i.e., the essential part, of the trademark. The term "crocodile" is evidently more convenient for Chinese members of the public to memorize and refer to. The allegedly infringing mark is similar to the crocodile trademark over which the appellant enjoys the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. The first-instance court's finding that the allegedly infringing mark is not similar to the crocodile trademark over which the appellant enjoys the exclusive right to use a registered trademark violates the general principles for determining trademark similarity. 2. The "single crocodile figure" in the allegedly infringing trademark is identical to the appellant's crocodile trademark. The "coexistence" agreement reached by the parties abroad in 1983 applies only to five countries and regions and cannot serve as a reason for the appellee's lawful use of the crocodile trademark in mainland China. Moreover, Chinese law does not recognize trademark coexistence. The first-instance judgment misconstrued the content and legal effect of that agreement. The trademark that the appellant alleges to be infringing is the "single crocodile figure" and the combined mark containing a crocodile figure; the appellant has not claimed that the overall packaging form of the allegedly infringing goods constitutes trademark infringement. To determine whether a trademark is infringed, the appellant's registered trademark pattern should be compared one by one with the allegedly infringing trademark pattern. The simultaneous use of "other marks" together with the infringing trademark on the allegedly infringing goods cannot result in the lawful use of the crocodile mark. The first-instance judgment's reasoning for non-infringement, that the allegedly infringing goods bear multiple trademark marks and, when considered together with the overall packaging, can be distinguished from the appellant's "crocodile" trademark, is logically at most relevant only to the time the consumer actually purchases the goods. However, after purchasing clothing and other goods, consumers do not wear the packaging or hangtags. At the time of actual purchase, the single crocodile is very prominent, and its use after sale is even more pronounced. Furthermore, an act of trademark infringement does not become lawful merely because it is large in scale and long in duration. The first-instance judgment's so-called "objective establishment of a specific commercial reputation" by the appellee is precisely the result of riding on the reputation of the appellant's trademark in bad faith. The appellant believes that the first-instance judgment contains significant errors and seriously damages the appellant's legitimate rights. It requests this Court to amend the judgment according to law and support all its claims in the first instance.

The appellees, Crocodile International and Shanghai Oriental Crocodile, responded: 1. In the final administrative judgments of the Beijing High People's Court, (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 178 and No. 277, which have already taken effect, it was clearly determined that when comparing Crocodile International's "CARTELO and device" trademark with Lacoste's "crocodile figure" and "crocodile figure + LACOSTE" trademarks, the graphic parts are similar, but the main parts and the overall structure of the combination of elements are not identical or similar. When observed in isolation under normal attention of the general public, and considering the distinctiveness and fame of Lacoste's crocodile figure trademark, some association may arise between them, but no confusion or misidentification will occur. The appellant's ground for appeal cannot stand. 2. Regarding whether the "single crocodile figure" in the allegedly infringing trademark constitutes an identical mark to the appellant's crocodile trademark. This case is different from ordinary trademark infringement cases. The dispute in this case has its specific historical background. Specifically: Lacoste's series of trademarks were first used in France around the 1930s and 1940s, gradually becoming known in Europe. Crocodile International's series of trademarks were first used in Singapore and elsewhere around the 1940s and 1950s, gradually becoming known in Asia. In the historical process of globalization of economic and trade activities, from the 1960s onward, Lacoste's series of trademarks were the first to seek entry into Asia, leading to repeated disputes and conflicts with Crocodile International's series of trademarks, which had already been registered, used, and become famous earlier in relevant Asian countries and regions. However, a settlement was eventually reached for the peaceful coexistence of the two parties' crocodile series of trademarks. On June 17, 1983, Crocodile International and Lacoste signed a comprehensive settlement agreement. In the agreement, the parties recognized that Lacoste's series of trademarks and Crocodile International's series of trademarks "may coexist in the relevant market without causing confusion." The agreement not only specified "cooperation in the countries listed in Article 1 of this Agreement" but also stated "where possible, cooperate in other parts of the world." The preamble of the settlement agreement stated that "the parties end and finally settle all pending legal disputes, legal actions, differences, disputes, and claims between them." In the more than 20 years since the signing of this settlement agreement, not only have Crocodile International's series of trademarks and Lacoste's series of trademarks achieved respective registration and peaceful coexistence in the five countries and regions listed in Article 1 of the agreement (Taiwan, China; Singapore; Indonesia; Malaysia; and Brunei), but also in other countries where Crocodile International registered earlier (e.g., South Korea, India, Pakistan, etc.), Crocodile International's series of trademarks and Lacoste's series of trademarks have achieved coexistence and mutual reinforcement. Because the parties' respective well-known trademarks "may coexist in the relevant market without causing confusion," each party actually possesses its own commercial reputation and product goodwill. Crocodile International does not have the subjective intent to "use Lacoste's brand reputation to cause consumer confusion or misidentification." Therefore, the standalone use of Crocodile International's single crocodile figure does not constitute infringement of Lacoste's single crocodile figure trademark. That is, "a mere crocodile figure" is also not infringing. Furthermore, when used in combination with the "CARTELO" text and the "CARTELO and device" trademark, the distinctiveness for differentiation is even more enhanced. In summary, in terms of graphics and text, there is a fact that the Crocodile International trademark and the Lacoste trademark are "not cause for confusion." Historically, there is a consensus that the Crocodile International trademark and the Lacoste trademark are "not cause for confusion." In practice, there is a reality that the Crocodile International trademark and the Lacoste trademark are "not cause for confusion." In the Chinese market, after large-scale, long-term, and comparative joint use, Lacoste's series of trademarks and Crocodile International's series of trademarks have formed and are increasingly strengthening the distinctiveness each has acquired, making them more and more clearly distinguishable without causing confusion. The appellees request this Court to uphold the first-instance judgment and dismiss the appellant's appeal.

During the proceedings before this Court, Lacoste, to support its appeal, submitted to this Court the decision of the Australian Trademark Office dated October 31, 2008, rejecting Crocodile International's trademark applications No. 1005106 and No. 1017333 in that country, certain correspondence between representatives of Lacoste and Crocodile International, excerpts from the book "Well-Known Trademarks and China's Well-Known Trademark Protection System," the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board (TRAB) of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China's Review Decision No. (2009) 15729 on trademark opposition, and the Trademark Office's Opposition Decisions (2005) Trademark Opposition Zi No. 0430 and (2008) Trademark Opposition Zi No. 10236 and their announcements, among other evidence. Subsequently, it also provided to this Court a mediation agreement between it and (Hong Kong) Crocodile Garments Co., Ltd. and Zhejiang Zhongda Crocodile Apparel Co., Ltd. in another case, the circumstances of its "crocodile figure" trademark registration in certain countries, and the Administrative Judgment (2009) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 736 and No. 732 of Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, the Civil Judgment (2009) Er Zhong Min Chu Zi No. 08129 of Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, the Civil Judgment (2008) Sui Zhong Fa Min San Zhong Zi No. 116 of Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province, and the Civil Judgment (2009) Zhe Zhi Zhong Zi No. 15 of the High People's Court of Zhejiang Province, for this Court's reference in hearing this case.

Crocodile International, to support its defense, submitted to this Court the 1971 judgment of the Osaka District Court and the 1973 mediation decision of the Osaka High Court in Japan, the 2006 judgment of the Paris Tribunal de Grande Instance in France, correspondence from Crocodile International's French agent reporting on the progress of the case before the Paris Tribunal de Grande Instance, a summary of the number and categories of Crocodile International's single crocodile trademark registrations in certain countries and regions, along with trademark registration certificates issued by the relevant countries, correspondence from 1982-1983 in which Lacoste acknowledged that the two parties' trademarks could coexist, seven letters of acknowledgment from Lacoste from 1985-1995, and two letters of acknowledgment from Crocodile International's predecessor, Leeseng Meng (利生民公司), from 1985, a statistical table of the coexistence of the two crocodile trademarks in the five countries and regions listed in the 1983 settlement agreement and in some countries and regions not listed, the decision of the Industrial Property Office of the Republic of Mauritius dated December 21, 2007, confirming that the two parties' trademarks could coexist, an explanation of the historical connection between Crocodile International and Hong Kong Crocodile Garments, and an explanation of the historical connection between Hong Kong Crocodile Garments and Lacoste, among other documents.

Regarding the evidence submitted by Lacoste, Crocodile International presented its objections during cross-examination: 1. As to the decision of the Australian Trademark Office, it did not recognize its authenticity, legality, or relevance. It argued that the background in Australia is exactly opposite to that in China. Australia has blood or kinship ties with Europe and France, being more influenced by Europe and France and less by Asia and Singapore, and Lacoste's crocodile brand entered earlier and has been used more widely there. In China, the opposite is true: it is more influenced by Asia and Singapore and less by Europe and France. In China, Lacoste's crocodile trademark, registered in 1980, was not used on a commercial scale for a long time. Instead, it was Crocodile International's trademark that was first commercialized, used on a large scale, and became known earlier. Crocodile International's applications for registration of the "CROCODILE and device" trademark have been approved in many countries worldwide. Even if not approved in Australia, this cannot be taken as representative of the whole to deny the many approvals elsewhere. 2. Regarding the correspondence between the representatives of the two companies, Crocodile International argued that Lacoste could not produce the originals in court, so their authenticity could not be confirmed. Because the correspondence was incomplete and contained errors in stating key fact dates, it believed there were obvious signs of forgery in the evidence. Additionally, the evidence had not undergone the necessary notarization and legalization procedures, so it did not recognize its authenticity, legality, or relevance. 3. As to the excerpts from "Well-Known Trademarks and China's Well-Known Trademark Protection System" provided by Lacoste, Crocodile International acknowledged the formal authenticity of the book and its page 497 but argued that this evidence was insufficient to prove that Lacoste's trademark was well-known at the time, and therefore did not recognize the truthfulness, legality, or relevance of the facts sought to be proven. 4. Regarding the evidence submitted by Lacoste, including the Trademark Opposition Decision (2008) Trademark Opposition Zi No. 10236 and its announcement, the Trademark Opposition Decision (2005) Trademark Opposition Zi No. 00430 regarding the trademark "尼罗鳄鱼 NI LU YU and device," the Review Decision on Trademark Opposition (2009) TRAB Review No. 15729 regarding the trademark "尼罗鳄鱼 NI LU YU and device" under Application No. 1653330, and the related trademark inquiry information and announcements, Crocodile International argued that the facts of the cases involved in those decisions were entirely different in background and circumstances from this case, and the two cases were not comparable. Therefore, this evidence had no relevance to the present case.

Regarding the evidentiary materials submitted by Crocodile International, Lacoste presented its objections during cross-examination, arguing that the 1983 settlement agreement was irrelevant to this case. The specific reasons are as follows: First, the agreement does not apply territorially to mainland China. In 1983, in order to enter the Asian market, Lacoste signed a settlement agreement with Crocodile International's predecessor, Leeseng Meng, paying USD 1.5 million to enter the five Asian countries and regions where it had pre-registered its trademarks, including Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan, China. The starting point of this agreement was to respect the pre-existing registered trademark rights. Only by obtaining the consent of the right holder through negotiation would infringement not result. Second, the premise of the agreement was a settlement in the case of trademark similarity. The "no confusion shall arise" stipulated in the agreement was directed at the parties themselves; in essence, it was based on the right holder's recognition and consent. Whether the public is confused is an objective fact that cannot be contractually stipulated by third parties. Third, the agreement resolved the coexistence issue in the countries and regions where Crocodile International had obtained registrations and had nothing to do with the scope of Lacoste's trademark registrations. Fourth, the intention to cooperate mentioned in the agreement pertained only to matters of trademark anti-counterfeiting and did not involve trademark coexistence. As to Crocodile International's claim that it had registered a single crocodile trademark in some countries and regions outside the agreement, Lacoste argued that, after the 1983 settlement agreement, the disputes concerning the two parties' crocodile trademarks were still resolved on a case-by-case basis. From an international perspective, Lacoste's "single crocodile figure" trademark had been registered in many countries, including China, decades before Crocodile International's first trademark application. Crocodile International had only obtained registration in a small number of Asian countries and regions. In the matter of registration and use of crocodile trademarks, the parties had always adopted different solutions based on specific circumstances. Moreover, before the litigation in this case, neither in China nor abroad had Crocodile International ever asserted the global coexistence of crocodile trademarks based on the 1983 settlement agreement. In previous litigations in different countries, judgments were made in accordance with the principle of territoriality of trademarks and based on the specific trademark situations of the parties in those particular countries, without being influenced by foreign factors.

With respect to the above evidence and related evidentiary materials, except for the decision of the Australian Trademark Office and the correspondence between the representatives of the two companies submitted by Lacoste, whose authenticity was denied by Crocodile International, neither Lacoste nor Crocodile International raised objections to the authenticity of the other evidence and related evidentiary materials. However, both parties raised objections to the relevance of the above evidence and related evidentiary materials to this case. Because this relevance primarily concerns this Court's determination of issues such as the well-known status of Lacoste's crocodile trademark, the circumstances of the registration of the two parties' crocodile figure trademarks in relevant countries and regions, and the impact of the 1983 settlement agreement on the relevant facts and legal issues of this case, this Court will make a comprehensive determination in the part on fact-finding and reasoning.

Upon examination and verification by this Court, the facts found by the first-instance court are substantially true and are hereby confirmed by this Court. Based on the evidence submitted by the parties in the first instance and the supplementary evidence and related documents submitted to this Court, this Court further finds the following facts: In 1933, Lacoste registered a crocodile figure trademark in France. On December 13, 1951, Leeseng Meng registered a crocodile figure trademark in Singapore for goods in Class 25. On October 26 of the same year, Leeseng Meng registered a crocodile figure trademark in Hong Kong for goods in Class 25. In 1952, 1953, and 1954, Leeseng Meng registered a crocodile figure trademark in India, Sarawak, Sabah (state), Malaysia, and other countries and regions for goods in Class 25. On April 27, 1959, Leeseng Meng registered a crocodile figure trademark in Japan.

In September 1994, Lacoste established its first counter at Shanghai Xujiahui Pacific Department Store. In June 1995, it established a second counter at the Shanghai Beijing Road Friendship Store. In August 1996, it established its first flagship store in Shanghai, the Shanghai Wanli Store. In 1997, it opened seven flagship stores or counters in Hangzhou, Nanjing, Kunming, Xi'an, and other cities. Thereafter, Lacoste successively established counters and flagship stores in Shanghai, Beijing, Qingdao, Dalian, and other cities. As of June 30, 1999, it had 13 flagship stores, 43 counters, and 1 retail store. In 1994, Crocodile International opened its first flagship store in Shanghai on South Shaanxi Road near the intersection with Huaihai Road. In 1995, it opened 85 flagship stores or counters in Shanghai (at the intersection of Huaihai Road and Maoming Road), Wuhan (third floor of Wuhan Plaza, No. 358 Jiefang Avenue), Guangzhou (Tianmiananshang, second floor of Tianhe City Plaza, No. 208 Tianhe Road), and in Jiangxi, Xinjiang, Shandong, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Yunnan, Fujian, and other places. In 1996, it opened 89 flagship stores or counters in Liaoning, Hebei, Jiangsu, Shandong, Anhui, and other places. By 1997, Crocodile International had a total of 250 flagship stores or counters nationwide.

Lishimin Co., Ltd. filed a civil lawsuit with the Osaka District Court in 1969, accusing the distributor of Lacoste, Sankyo Seiko Co., Ltd., of infringing its trademark rights. In that case, the composition of Lishimin's trademark consisted of: "Within a rectangular frame having a length-to-width ratio of 3:8, the English word 'Crocodile' is written from the lower left corner upward toward the right, and a crocodile figure almost parallel to the letters is drawn, with its head pointing downward, tail upward, and mouth slightly open." The alleged infringing acts were stated as: "The Lacoste shirts imported and sold by the defendant bear a mark as shown in Appendix (A) [Appendix (i)] — hereinafter referred to as Mark (A). The mark used on the left chest area is as shown in Appendix (B) — hereinafter referred to as Mark (B). Mark (B) [Appendix (u)] depicts a green crocodile with its head facing right, and the words 'Lacoste' in black on its body. Mark (A) has the words 'CHEMISE LACOSTE' at the top, combined with the figure, not just the crocodile figure alone." Lishimin sought an injunction prohibiting the defendant from using Marks (A), (B), and (C), payment of 1,000,000 yen in damages, and delayed interest at 5% per annum from May 15, 1969, until the said amount was paid in full.

On February 24, 1971, the Osaka District Court rendered Judgment No. 2333 of 1969 (Nen). In that judgment, the Osaka District Court held: "Indeed, as the plaintiff asserts, the crocodile figure is very prominent in the trademark at issue, and the word '[CROCODILE]' is merely the name of that figure. However, given that the trademarks (1)-(8) mentioned above already existed and the trademark at issue was later, it is essentially clear that a crocodile figure alone is not sufficient for differentiation from the said trademarks. Regardless of how one considers it, in order to achieve the distinguishing function of a trademark, it is necessary for the crocodile figure to be combined with text, thereby giving the trademark at issue distinctiveness. Despite the existence of the aforesaid trademarks (1)-(8), the trademark at issue was still registered. This does not indicate that it merely generated the name and concept of the 'Crocodile' brand; rather, it is the overall combination of the figure and the text that gives it distinctiveness, enabling it to be distinguished from other trademarks that also use a crocodile image."

"Now let us compare the composition of the trademark at issue with Marks (A), (B), and (C) [the original Japanese drawings (ィ), (ロ), (ハ); the English translation lacks drawings (ィ) and (ロ)]. Mark (A) is designed as a crocodile figure facing right (body in green, open mouth in red), with the black word '[LACOSTE]' embedded in the body. Mark (B) is designed as a crocodile figure facing right (body in yellow, open mouth in red). Mark (C) is designed as a crocodile figure facing right, with its tail up and mouth open. The defendant does not use Marks (A), (B), or (C) alone, but rather in combination with text. Even if the defendant used Marks (A), (B), and (C) as claimed by the plaintiff, needless to say, they are different from the trademark at issue. Moreover, the trademark at issue only possesses distinctiveness when the crocodile figure and the text are combined as a whole. Marks (A), (B), and (C) do not contain the word 'crocodile,' and they are not similar to the trademark at issue in terms of appearance, name, or concept. Therefore, it can be concluded that the defendant's use of the said marks does not infringe any rights of the trademark at issue. The premise that the use of the so-called Marks (A), (B), and (C) allegedly constitutes an infringement of the plaintiff's trademark rights, which forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim, is not established and must be dismissed."

On November 28, 1973, the parties reached a settlement at the Osaka High Court, whereby Lishimin agreed that Lacoste could register the "crocodile figure" trademark in Japan.

On June 1, 1982, in a letter from Mr. Michel Lacoste, then Chairman of the Board of Directors of Lacoste, to Mr. Chen Xianjin, founder of Crocodile International Co., Ltd., it was stated: "...Basically, we disagree that there is a substantial risk of confusion between our respective trademarks in these countries. Because of their long-term use in these markets, each has acquired distinctiveness. In fact, as you know, the courts in Japan and the Taiwan region of China held this view many years ago, and we believe that the courts in those countries where litigation is pending will also adopt this view."

On January 21, 1983, in a letter from Mr. Bernard Lacoste of Lacoste to Mr. Chen Xianjin, founder of Crocodile International Co., Ltd., it was stated: "...In Asian countries, the coexistence of our different crocodile trademarks is commercially feasible, just as it is in Japan..."

On June 17, 1983, the parties entered into a Settlement Agreement. After the execution of the Settlement Agreement, on August 22, 1985, Crocodile International Co., Ltd., at the request of Lacoste, issued a letter of undertaking, promising that when Lacoste applied to register the relevant crocodile figure trademarks in the Republic of Korea, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, Crocodile International would not raise trademark oppositions, invalidity or cancellation actions, and would issue appropriate letters of consent.

On August 7, 1985, Bernard Lacoste, General Manager of Lacoste, issued a letter of consent for Crocodile International Co., Ltd., agreeing to its registration of the crocodile figure trademark in the Republic of Korea for goods in Class 45. On January 22, 1993, Bernard Lacoste, General Manager of Lacoste, issued a letter of consent agreeing to the registration of the crocodile figure trademark in the Republic of Korea for goods in Class 25. On September 16, 1993, and January 18, 1994, respectively, Bernard Lacoste, General Manager of Lacoste, issued letters of consent agreeing to the registration of the crocodile figure trademark in Pakistan for goods in Classes 14, 9, 18, and 28.

Crocodile International Co., Ltd. registered a single crocodile trademark in Class 25 in Hong Kong on October 26, 1951; in Brunei on September 21, 1961; in Indonesia on April 28, 1970; in Sri Lanka on August 31, 1979; in the Republic of Korea on November 13, 1982; in the Taiwan region of China on November 16, 1982; in Thailand on August 13, 1985; in Mongolia on June 14, 1996; in Nepal on October 31, 1995; in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea on November 27, 1995; in Morocco on June 24, 2003; in Saudi Arabia on April 8, 2003; and in Fiji on September 1, 2003.

Furthermore, in 1994, Lacoste applied for registration in France of the two crocodile figures of Crocodile International Co., Ltd. (French Registration Nos. 94541293, 94541290) from the 1983 Agreement, as well as a left-facing Lacoste crocodile figure (French Registration No. 94541291). In 2005, Crocodile International filed a lawsuit with the Paris Tribunal de Grande Instance. On March 29, 2006, the court rendered its judgment. The judgment held: "Lacoste, while fully informed, imitated the two trademarks used by Crocodile International and registered them (Registration Nos. 94541293 and 94541290), intending to create the illusion of priority for its own trademarks in a country outside France and to counter the latter. This conduct constitutes an unlawful registration, as these registrations deviate from the legal function of trademarks and violate the cooperation agreed upon in the 1983 agreement between the parties, which is not limited to the five countries and regions specified therein." The judgment further held that "Lacoste's act of imitating the trademark designs of Crocodile International set forth in the agreement of June 17, 1983" constituted "an act of unlawful registration." The court ordered: "Rejects Crocodile International's request to declare Registration Nos. 94541290 and 94541293 invalid and the trademarks void, given that the two trademarks have been invalid since November 23, 2004; accepts the remaining requests. Declares that Lacoste's imitation of Crocodile International's trademark designs set forth in the agreement of June 17, 1983, and their registration (Registration Nos. 94541293 and 94541290) constitutes the offense of unlawful registration. Orders Lacoste to pay Crocodile International EUR 1 as damages. Permits Crocodile International to publish the present ruling in three newspapers or magazines of its choice, at Lacoste's expense, up to a maximum of EUR 4,500 after tax. Declares that the registration of trademark No. 94541291 is not unlawful. Accepts Crocodile International's request to declare this number invalid." Lacoste appealed.

On October 19, 1994, Lacoste applied in France for a trademark featuring a left-facing crocodile head. On March 23, 1995, it filed an application for territorial extension in China, with Application No. G638122, designating goods in Class 25, including clothing, footwear, and headwear. On June 26, 1996, the Trademark Office rejected the application on the ground that the crocodile figure trademark of Hong Kong Crocodile Garments Company was well-known to the public, and the differences between the Hong Kong "crocodile" and the French "crocodile" had been accepted by consumers, and that under Article 8(1)(9) of the former Trademark Law, the applied-for trademark had other adverse effects. On August 30, 1996, Lacoste applied for review with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board (TRAB), arguing that Lacoste, as the company that first designed the crocodile figure trademark in the world and first registered the crocodile figure trademark in China, was logically the prior rights holder of the crocodile trademark. The holder of the cited trademark, Crocodile Garments Company, although also using the crocodile figure trademark for many years, began using and registering the trademark from the 1950s, both internationally and in China, later than Lacoste, and had reached a mutual understanding memorandum with Crocodile Garments Company. Lacoste requested the TRAB to approve the registration of the applied-for trademark. On January 12, 2009, the TRAB issued a review decision, rejecting the application for territorial extension in China. On February 12, 2009, Lacoste filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. On December 29, 2009, that court rendered a first-instance judgment, revoking the TRAB's said decision. That case and related series of cases are currently under second-instance trial at the Beijing High People's Court.

In 1999, the Chengdu Administration for Industry and Commerce of Sichuan Province issued Notice (1999) No. 148 on the Closing of the Case Concerning the Crocodile Figure Trademark, determining that Sichuan Oriental Crocodile Company's separate use of the crocodile figure trademark constituted an infringement of Lacoste's crocodile figure trademark.

This Court further finds that, in the case concerning the administrative dispute over trademarks between Lacoste and the TRAB and Lufeng Jieshi Jingang Garment Factory, Lacoste was dissatisfied with the Beijing High People's Court's administrative judgment (2008) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 12 and applied to this Court for retrial. This Court's Notice of Rejection of Retrial Application (2009) Zhi Xing Zi No. 10 found: "Based on the available evidence, the evidence proving the fame of the cited trademarks before the filing date of the disputed trademark consists only of the promotional materials for sponsoring the Davis Cup tennis tournament in 1984 and the Trademark Office's Ruling (89) Shang Biao Yi Zi No. 116. Although the latter mentioned that the crocodile trademark had a certain degree of fame, taken together, this evidence is insufficient to establish that the cited trademarks were well known by the relevant public in China prior to the filing date of the disputed trademark (March 26, 1991), so as to be considered well-known trademarks." In the case concerning the administrative dispute over trademark opposition review between Lacoste and the TRAB and Crocodile International Co., Ltd., Lacoste was dissatisfied with the Beijing High People's Court's administrative judgments (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 277 and (2007) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 108, both rendered on December 20, 2007, and applied to this Court for retrial. This Court's Notices of Rejection of Retrial Application (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 121 and (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 107 found: "The available evidence in this case cannot establish that the cited trademarks were well known by the relevant public in China before the filing date of the opposed trademarks. On the basis of comparing the overall structures of the opposed trademarks and the cited trademarks, applying the ordinary attention of the relevant public and considering the distinctiveness and fame of the cited trademarks, the lower court's determination that the opposed trademarks and the cited trademarks were not similar trademarks was not erroneous." Accordingly, on October 30, 2009, it rejected Lacoste's retrial application on the ground that the grounds for retrial asserted by Lacoste were untenable.

The above facts are supported by evidence including: the statistical tables of respective specialty stores or counters submitted by Crocodile International and Lacoste; the translation of Judgment No. 2333 of 1969 (Nen) rendered by the Osaka District Court of Japan; the translation of the 1983 Settlement Agreement between Singapore Crocodile and French Crocodile; respective letters of consent; correspondence; Crocodile International's trademark registration certificates in relevant countries; the translation of Judgment No. 05/01245 rendered by the Paris Tribunal de Grande Instance; the translation of the October 31, 2008 decision of the Australian Trademark Office refusing Crocodile International's trademark applications No. 1005106 and No. 1017333 in Australia; the administrative judgments (2009) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 736 and No. 732 of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court; the Notice on the Closing of the Case Concerning the Crocodile Figure Trademark, Cheng Gong Shang Han (1999) No. 148, issued by the Chengdu Administration for Industry and Commerce of Sichuan Province; and this Court's Notices of Rejection of Retrial Application (2009) Zhi Xing Zi No. 10, (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 121, and (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 107.

Upon trial, the issues in dispute are summarized as follows: 1. Whether the Trademark Law revised on October 27, 2001 should apply to this case; 2. Whether the accused Marks 1 and 2 are similar to the registered trademarks for which Lacoste seeks protection; 3. Whether the accused Marks 3 and 4 are similar to the registered trademarks for which Lacoste seeks protection.

With respect to the above issues, this Court holds as follows:

(I) Regarding the issue of whether the Trademark Law revised on October 27, 2001 should apply to this case.

Because the appellant filed the lawsuit at first instance on May 11, 2000, and the alleged infringing acts of the appellee occurred in 1995, and the first instance court accepted the case before the effective date of the amendments to the Trademark Law revised on October 27, 2001, in accordance with Articles 8 and 9 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Issues Concerning the Jurisdiction and Application of Law in the Trial of Trademark Cases, this case should apply the Trademark Law before revision, while compensation issues may refer to Article 56 of the revised Trademark Law. The first instance court's application of the revised Trademark Law was improper, and this Court hereby corrects same.

(II) Regarding the issue of whether accused Marks 1 and 2 are similar trademarks to the registered trademarks for which Lacoste seeks protection.

Article 38(1) of the Trademark Law before revision provides that "using a trademark that is identical or similar to a registered trademark on the same or similar goods without the permission of the trademark registrant" constitutes an infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks provides: "'Similar trademarks' as referred to in Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law (referring to the Trademark Law revised on October 27, 2001 — footnote) means that the accused infringing trademark, when compared with the plaintiff's registered trademark, is similar in terms of the shape, pronunciation, or meaning of the characters, or the composition or color of the figure, or the overall structure of the combination of elements, or similar in three-dimensional shape or color combination, such that it is likely to cause the relevant public to be confused about the source of the goods or to believe that the source is specifically linked to the goods of the plaintiff's registered trademark." With reference to the said judicial interpretation and based on trial practice, determining whether the accused mark constitutes a similar trademark to the plaintiff's registered trademark within the meaning of Article 38(1) of the pre-revision Trademark Law generally requires an assessment of the similarity of the constituent elements of the marks in dispute, such as the shape, pronunciation, and meaning of the text or the composition and color of the figure, and considers the likelihood of confusion as an important factor. Therefore, trademark similarity in the context of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark refers to confusing similarity, i.e., similarity sufficient to cause market confusion. Given the complexity of the marks in dispute in different cases, in addition to considering the degree of similarity of their constituent elements, the determination of trademark similarity may also take into account other relevant factors based on the specific circumstances of the case, and on that basis determine whether the marks in dispute constitute confusing similarity. If the marks in dispute are similar in terms of constituent elements, but after comprehensive consideration of other relevant factors, it cannot be found that they are sufficient to cause market confusion, then they shall not be found to constitute similar trademarks within the meaning of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. In this case, among the registered trademarks for which Lacoste claims rights, its crocodile faces right, with its mouth wide open, and its torso and tail are covered with blocky scales or decorated with horizontal stripes, among which registered trademark No. 213407 also prominently bears the word LACOSTE below the crocodile figure. The accused Marks 1 and 2 used by Crocodile International feature a crocodile facing left; in accused Mark 1, the scales on the torso of the crocodile figure are three-dimensional; in accused Mark 2, the overall color of the crocodile figure is yellow-green or yellow, with its mouth open showing red, and oblique stripes on the torso. Compared with Lacoste's series of registered trademarks, accused Marks 1 and 2 both contain a crocodile figure and have a certain degree of similarity, but the direction of the crocodile's head, body shape, scales, and color in accused Marks 1 and 2 differ from the crocodile figures for which Lacoste claims rights. In particular, the trademarks in dispute between the parties have a specific formation history and development process in the relevant market, and have a particular coexistence and use status. In this case, determining whether the marks in dispute constitute similar trademarks within the meaning of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark requires neither a separation from each party's own formation and development history, nor a disregard of the coexistence process and use status between the parties. Otherwise, it would be difficult to reach a fair and reasonable adjudication. Therefore, given the specific circumstances of the marks in dispute in this case, when determining their similarity, it is insufficient to merely compare the similarity of the marks themselves; it is also necessary to comprehensively consider factors such as Crocodile International's subjective intent, the history and current status of coexistence and use between the parties, and combine this with the actual market situation to make a fair and reasonable determination.

First, based on the facts already found in this case, the predecessor of Crocodile International Co. was Liming Seng Company, founded by Chen Xianjin in Singapore in 1943. That company applied for and obtained registration of the "crocodile + crocodile device" and "crocodile device" trademarks in Singapore in 1949, with registration granted in 1951. The products of Liming Seng Company entered Hong Kong in 1953 and were primarily sold in the Southeast Asian region. Based on the existing evidence and taking into account the international economic conditions in 1949 and the fact that Lacoste Co. only began entering the Asian market in the 1960s, it is insufficient to conclude that Liming Seng Company at that time applied for registration of the "crocodile + crocodile device" trademark by copying or imitating the relevant trademarks applied for by Lacoste Co. After entering the Chinese market, Crocodile International Co. continued to use the relevant crocodile identifiers corresponding to trademarks already registered in relevant Asian countries. Furthermore, according to the facts found by the trial court, Crocodile International Co. used the "CARTELO and device" trademark on the outer packaging and product hangtags of the accused infringing products 1-8; on accused infringing products 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6, the "CARTELO and device" trademark was used on the collar or waistband, on the back of the tie in the gift box of accused infringing product 7, and on the inner sole of the women's shoes of accused infringing product 8; on the front of the leather bag of accused infringing product 3, on the front of the wallet in the gift box of accused infringing product 7, and on the front of the belt buckle, the wording "CARTELO" was used. The environment and state of use of the accused identifiers are sufficient to make the relevant products of the two parties clearly distinguishable. The above facts sufficiently indicate that after Crocodile International Co. entered the Chinese market, its use of the relevant trademarks primarily constituted a continuation of its existing trademarks, and in actual use it also intentionally distinguished the disputed identifiers. Therefore, the trial court's determination that the conduct of Crocodile International Co. differed from the counterfeit conduct of deliberately imitating famous luxury brands, and that it subjectively had no intention of exploiting Lacoste Co.'s brand reputation to cause consumer confusion or misidentification, was not improper, and the relevant claims of the appellant are unsupported by evidence.

Second, from the perspective of the relevant international market, the disputed identifiers of the two parties have long formed an international market pattern of coexistence and use in some countries and regions in Asia. Based on the facts already found in this case, the predecessor of Crocodile International Co., Liming Seng Company, registered a relevant crocodile device trademark in Singapore on December 13, 1951, in Class 25. On October 26 of the same year, Liming Seng Company registered a relevant crocodile device trademark in Hong Kong in Class 25, and entered the Hong Kong market in 1953. On April 27, 1959, Liming Seng Company registered a relevant crocodile device trademark in Japan. In 1969, Crocodile International Co. filed a lawsuit in the Osaka District Court of Japan against Lacoste Co. for infringement of its crocodile device trademark rights. The two companies later reached a settlement agreement in the High Court of Japan, resulting in the 1983 Settlement Agreement. That Settlement Agreement confirmed that the relevant identifiers of the two companies could coexist without causing confusion in the relevant countries and regions. Because, prior to this lawsuit, accused identifiers 1 and 2 of Crocodile International Co. had been registered for many years in relevant countries and regions, and a 1983 Settlement Agreement had been reached with Lacoste Co. confirming that the identifiers including accused identifiers 1 and 2 and Lacoste Co.'s crocodile device and word series identifiers could coexist without causing confusion, and in countries not explicitly listed in that agreement, such as South Korea and Pakistan, Lacoste Co. also issued letters of consent agreeing to the registration of the accused identifiers in the relevant classes in those two countries. In light of this, this Court considers that, whether from the perspective of the relevant recognition and consensus of the parties or from the actual international market situation, the disputed identifiers of the two parties are unlikely to cause market confusion in some countries and regions in Asia and can coexist. This sufficiently indicates that the similarity in constituent elements of the disputed trademarks does not necessarily constitute confusing similarity and does not necessarily preclude their coexistence. Because the geographical scope explicitly listed in the 1983 Settlement Agreement signed by the parties does not cover Mainland China, the trial court's direct confirmation of its validity was improper, but it was not impermissible to consider it as an important factor in determining that the disputed identifiers could coexist.

Third, from the perspective of the coexistence and use of the disputed identifiers in the Chinese market, both have their own relevant public in the Chinese market, have formed objective divisions in the market, and have become distinguishable identifiers. In this case, Lacoste Co.'s products formally entered China in 1984, but in limited quantities. Both companies began opening counters or specialty stores in China from 1994. According to the facts already found in this case, Lacoste Co.'s crocodile trademark did not have high popularity in China at that time. In contrast, after Crocodile International Co. entered the Chinese market, its business scale expanded rapidly. In 1995 alone, it had opened 85 specialty stores or counters in places such as Shanghai, Wuhan, Guangzhou, Jiangxi, Xinjiang, Shandong, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Yunnan, and Fujian. In 1996, it opened another 89 specialty stores or counters in Liaoning, Hebei, Jiangsu, Shandong, and Anhui. Its popularity and influence rapidly increased, and it acquired a relatively stable customer base. In comparison, by the end of 1996, Lacoste Co. had only three specialty stores (counters) in China. Furthermore, the price difference between the products of Crocodile International Co. and those of Lacoste Co. is quite apparent; each has its own distinct consumer base. Moreover, the sales channels for the products of both companies are specialty stores or counters, and accused identifiers 1 and 2 are used in actual practice together with other relevant identifiers to designate the goods, thereby creating a unique use state that facilitates distinguishing the source of the goods. These factors are sufficient to show that the accused identifiers have formed a fixed association with the goods they respectively designate within their respective relevant markets, are sufficiently independent to indicate the source of their goods, and will not lead to the improper erosion of Lacoste Co.'s market share. The disputing parties have formed mutually independent market patterns in the relevant market. This is the objective basis sufficient to determine that the disputed trademarks can be distinguished. Considering the above factors comprehensively, given that Crocodile International Co. did not have the malicious intent to plagiarize or imitate when using the accused identifiers, this objective distinction formed through market competition is the result of Crocodile International Co.'s commercial success in China, which should be legally recognized and affirmed. Therefore, it should be considered that although accused identifiers 1 and 2 are similar to Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks, the relevant public has objectively distinguished the disputed identifiers of the two companies, and their coexistence is insufficient to cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of their goods. This is the first point. Second, the actual value of a trademark lies in distinguishing the source of goods, not in simply allowing the trademark owner to exclusively monopolize specific identifier symbols. Where the source of goods can be actually distinguished, even if the accused identifier or its main constituent elements have a certain degree of similarity to the registered trademark, it should not be determined to constitute a similar trademark in the sense of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark; otherwise, it would depart from the legislative intent of the Trademark Law in protecting trademark rights. It is precisely based on the market reality that Crocodile International Co.'s products have formed their own relevant consumer groups and the relevant public has objectively distinguished the relevant products of the two companies that this Court considers that accused identifiers 1 and 2 do not constitute similar trademarks to the registered trademarks for which Lacoste Co. seeks protection. Third, in the specific judgment on infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, treating whether it is sufficient to create market confusion as an important consideration for determining trademark similarity primarily requires that the relevant identifiers have a high probability of not creating market confusion; it does not require reaching the degree that no person will ever misidentify under any circumstances. This is especially true when determining whether relevant commercial identifiers that have certain similar elements due to complex historical origins and current states are similar. Therefore, although the presence of certain similar elements in the pronunciation and devices of accused identifiers 1 and 2 in this case does not rule out the possibility that some consumers may misidentify them, this does not detract from the overall distinctiveness of the identifiers themselves resulting from the above factors.

In summary, based on the comparison of the constituent elements of accused identifier 1 and accused identifier 2 with Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks seeking protection, as well as the development history and coexistence status of the parties and other relevant factors, this Court also determines that accused identifier 1 and accused identifier 2 do not constitute confusing similarity in the sense of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark against Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks seeking protection, and are insufficient to cause damage to Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks. Therefore, the trial court's conclusion that "Crocodile International Co.'s use of the 'crocodile device' alone on accused infringing products 1-8 also does not infringe Lacoste Co.'s exclusive right to use its registered trademark" was not improper. The appellant's claim that the above trademarks constitute identical trademarks cannot be upheld.

Of course, given that this Court has made its determination on the issue of similarity of the disputed trademarks based on a comprehensive consideration of the differences in constituent elements of the disputed identifiers, especially relevant factors such as the history of use and the status of coexistence, and since accused identifiers 1 and 2 do have a certain degree of similarity in their constituent elements to Lacoste Co.'s relevant registered trademarks, Crocodile International Co., when using accused identifiers 1 and 2, should maintain a relevant environment and state of use that clearly distinguishes them from Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks and should avoid Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks as much as possible.

(3) Whether accused identifiers 3 and 4 are similar to the registered trademarks for which Lacoste Co. seeks protection.

In this case, accused identifiers 3 and 4 consist of a single crocodile combined with the wording CARTELO. Compared with the registered trademarks for which Lacoste Co. seeks protection, there are obvious differences in wording composition, pronunciation, and overall appearance. Furthermore, in the trademark administrative dispute cases already concluded by this Court, namely (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 107, (2009) Xing Jian Zi No. 121, and (2009) Zhi Xing Zi No. 10, this Court has already found that Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks seeking protection were not yet well-known in China in 1994 and 1995, and determined that the opposed trademarks were not similar to Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks seeking protection. In light of this, this Court considers that accused identifiers 3 and 4 are significantly different from Lacoste Co.'s registered trademarks seeking protection and cannot be determined to be similar trademarks in the sense of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. The trial court's determination that "it is found that the 'CARTELO and device' and 'crocodile device' trademarks and the 'crocodile device + LACOSTE' trademark will not cause confusion or misidentification... the use of the 'CARTELO and device' trademark on the outer packaging and product hangtags of accused infringing products 1-8 did not infringe Lacoste Co.'s exclusive right to use its registered trademark" was not improper, and Lacoste Co.'s appellate reason that the two should be determined as similar trademarks also cannot be upheld.

In conclusion, Lacoste Co.'s grounds of appeal cannot be upheld. The facts found by the trial court were basically clear. Although the trial court's application of the pre-amendment Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China to adjudicate this case was erroneous in law, and some reasoning was improper, this did not affect the outcome of the case. This Court affirms the judgment. Pursuant to Article 153, Items (1) and (2), of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The court acceptance fee for the first instance and the second instance, each RMB 25,010, shall be borne by Lacoste Co., (France).

This judgment is final.
